assertion: The rate of babies receiving a dose of hepatitis B vaccine at birth has fallen from 80.0% from 2020 to 2022 to just 65.6% this year after federal advisers downgraded the preventive measure last year
inaccuracy: The claim says the fall came 'after' the downgrade; the paper says the decline began in mid-2023 and predated the vote, and the sample is Truveta EHR, not national.
measure: hepatitis B birth dose vaccination newborns

assertion: of which 0.18% were positive for HBV antibodies (HBsAg)
inaccuracy: The claim says antibodies; the paper says HBsAg-positive, a surface antigen. The 0.18% figure is right.
why_not: The 0.18% passage in the paper confirms the figure but calls the marker HBsAg-positive, not antibody-positive, so the figure matches while the label is wrong.

assertion: They analyzed data on 1.3 million infants born to 1.1 million women. Of the pregnancies, 90.5% had evidence of an HBV test
The proportion of mothers with no test recorded during pregnancy was 15.6% in 2018 and 7.6% in 2026.
Over the study period, 1,016,149 newborns (75.9%) received hepatitis B vaccination within a day of birth.

Newborn vaccination rates were 96.9% over the study period in babies whose mothers tested positive for HBV infection, compared with 75.9% among mothers who tested negative, 76.8% among mothers who had an unknown status, and 75.4% among those with no evidence of a test.

Hepatitis B vaccination rates were 97% to 98% for infants born to mothers who tested positive for HBsAg during pregnancy from 2018 through 2025, but that rate dropped to 93.9% from January through June 2026.
about 360,000 infants each year are born to mothers who aren't screen for the virus
reason: This is the authors' estimate (applying a 90% screening rate to about 3.6M births), and the arithmetic matches. 'No evidence of screening' in EHR is not proof of no screening.

assertion: more than 640 infants a year are born to mothers with a hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection who are not tested
reason: Estimate that matches the paper's arithmetic.

assertion: Almost a year ago, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices voted to replace a universal recommendation for the hepatitis B vaccine at birth—which had been in place since 1991—with individual decision-making for infants of mothers who test negative for HBV without presenting data to support the decision.
inaccuracy: The claim says no data was presented to support the decision; CIDRAP's own vote story says the meeting included risk-benefit discussion and only quotes Hibbeln saying no science was presented on the before-or-after-two-months timing point.

assertion: The decision came on the heels of a report by the Vaccine Integrity Project (VIP) demonstrating the safety, effectiveness, and public health benefits of the birth dose. The VIP is led by the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy
independent_value: VIP report dated Dec 2, 2025 (3 days before the vote); supported by CIDRAP unrestricted gift; authors from UMN-CIDRAP
reason: Report exists and is dated before the vote; the article discloses the CIDRAP link. 'Demonstrating' is the report's own conclusion.

assertion: That schedule reduced the number of recommended routine vaccines from 17 to 11, though a federal judge in March blocked the changes.
